subject: physics
question_text: Define specific heat capacity of a substance. What is its value for water?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 13 Very Short Answer Question 11 (printed p.137). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by one kelvin; for water this is 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, equivalently 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Definition
lines: The specific heat capacity of a
substance is the heat needed to
steps.margin_note: First mark. The words unit mass and one kelvin both carry it.
steps.why: Different substances need different amounts of heat to warm up by the same amount, so the heat is stated per unit mass and per one kelvin rise to make it a fixed property of the substance.
common_mistakes: Saying it is the heat needed to raise the temperature, without naming unit mass and one kelvin.

recall.must_convey: That specific heat capacity is the heat needed to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by one kelvin.
accept: heat needed to raise unit mass by one kelvin
heat per unit mass per kelvin rise
heat required for one kelvin rise in unit mass

steps.memory_tip: Specific means per unit mass. Heat capacity means heat needed for one kelvin rise.

steps.label: Value for water
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Give the value with its unit; the SI form 4186 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the one to write, and 1 cal g⁻¹ °C⁻¹ is the same number.
steps.why: Water needs an unusually large amount of heat to warm up compared with most substances, which is why its specific heat capacity is a commonly quoted number in the SI unit J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
common_mistakes: Writing the value as 4186 J without the kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ unit.
Confusing this number with the latent heat of water, which is a different quantity.

recall.must_convey: That the specific heat capacity of water is 4186 joule per kilogram per kelvin, the same as 1 calorie per gram per degree Celsius.
accept: 1 calorie per gram per degree Celsius
four one eight six J kg inverse K inverse
reject: heat needed to raise unit mass by one kelvin

steps.memory_tip: Water's number, 4186, is worth remembering as 1 calorie per gram per degree Celsius.

insider_note: Two marks means the definition AND the number — a bare 4186 with no definition loses the first mark.
